query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a rapid reaction synthesis method—specifically spark plasma sintering (SPS)—enables large‐scale processing of refractory high-entropy alloy composites with Cu while limiting excessive interdiffusion from the positive heat of mixing, thus achieving a stable microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous powder mixture of refractory alloying elements (e.g., Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W) and Cu in the desired near-equiatomic ratios.
generation.intervention: Application of SPS with controlled rapid heating and a short dwell time under inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, rapid consolidation conditions that minimize the time for diffusion between Cu and refractory elements, preventing extensive intermixing due to the positive enthalpy of mixing.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in-situ reactive interface during rapid densification that preserves distinct phases while promoting interfacial bonding.
generation.mechanism: SPS rapidly heats the powder compact, causing a self-propagating reaction that permits local phase formation and densification before significant diffusion occurs, thereby circumventing the problematic mixing enthalpy between Cu and the refractory elements.
generation.predicted_outcome: A composite microstructure with well‐defined refractory and Cu domains that maintains high strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability, while mitigating phase instability issues seen in conventional sintering.
generation.baseline: Composite structures produced via conventional sintering or melting techniques that allow prolonged diffusion, resulting in unstable microstructures due to excessive mixing.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective only if the sintering parameters (temperature, pressure, dwell time) are tightly controlled; excessive temperature or time may negate the benefits by allowing too much diffusion.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvements in mechanical and irradiation properties are uncertain and depend on precise process optimization and alloy composition; further experimental parameter tuning is required to quantify the benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of composite samples from the same refractory alloy and Cu powder mix. Process one set using spark plasma sintering (SPS) with rapid heating and short dwell times, and the other using a conventional sintering method with longer dwell times. Compare the microstructural features, phase distributions, and mechanical properties of both sets.
measurements: Scanning and transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for microstructure analysis
Thermal stability tests under high-temperature conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed samples do not exhibit significantly finer and more stable microstructures with improved mechanical or thermal properties compared to those from conventional sintering, then the hypothesis that SPS can overcome the mixing challenges is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
